fixes.wrong: “And the whole complaint remains addressed to “my God, my God,” twice: the forsaking is real, and so is the relationship it's spoken into.” Moves from felt abandonment to an unqualified account of forsaking despite the essay's restraint.
fixes.proposed: The complaint remains addressed to ‘my God, my God’: the anguish is real, and the sufferer still brings it to God. The cry does not explain everything God is doing.

fixes.wrong: “But he is not a bystander to it. From his first steps toward Jerusalem he told his own followers plainly what he was going toward (Matthew 16:21; 20:18-19), and in Gethsemane the night before he did not flinch from it (26:39). This wasn't a thing that happened to him — it's the thing he came to do, carried on purpose, by the one who chose to carry it.” Willing suffering still happens to its sufferer; did not flinch is unsupported here.
fixes.proposed: Yeshua’s willing self-giving does not make this anguish less real. Here he cries out to God in the words of Psalm 22; we need not explain away that lament to confess his purpose.

fixes.wrong: “Matthew isn't claiming Hosea secretly forecast this journey — he's showing that Yeshua doesn't stand apart from Israel's story but takes it up and embodies it.” Categorically excludes a further prophetic intention; flag informed by my knowledge of interpretive debate.
fixes.proposed: Hosea’s words look back to Israel’s exodus. Matthew applies them to Yeshua’s return from Egypt, presenting him as embodying Israel’s story. Christians differ over how this pattern relates to prophecy; the correspondence itself is clear.

fixes.wrong: “The market filled the outer court — the space where the nations could draw near — so Isaiah’s welcome and Jeremiah’s warning name a single failure: the place meant for others’ access to God had become a refuge for self-interest.” Study expressly says Mark does not specify the geography.
fixes.proposed: Yeshua brings Isaiah’s welcome and Jeremiah’s warning together: God’s house is for the nations’ prayer, yet it has become a robbers’ refuge. Some interpreters connect this with commerce in the outer court; Mark does not specify that location here.

fixes.wrong: “But if your confinement has someone's hands on it, that's not this verse: the fish was God's appointment, not a captor's, and that confinement is something to get free of, not sit inside.” Unsupported universal distinction about human-caused confinement.
fixes.proposed: This story does not tell you to remain where someone is harming or controlling you. Seeking safety and help is compatible with trusting God’s care.

fixes.wrong: ““Three days and three nights” was an ordinary Jewish way of counting any part of a day as a day, so Friday to Sunday honestly fits the idiom.” States settled harmonization despite study's caveat and missing historical witnesses.
fixes.proposed: A common explanation relates ‘three days and three nights’ to inclusive counting of days. How that explains the nights remains debated; this verse itself gives the comparison with Jonah, not a detailed chronology.

fixes.wrong: “Let this verse's fear stay a fear today, rather than resolving it into comfort too quickly.” Makes sustained fear the task.
fixes.proposed: Take this warning seriously by naming any deliberate turning away from Christ that needs an honest response. Ordinary doubt is not the same thing; bring that to God honestly too.

fixes.wrong: “Hagar — an enslaved Egyptian woman in the wilderness — is the only person Scripture records giving God a name: El Roi, “God of seeing,” heard down the centuries as “the God who sees me” — and a few words later she says exactly that: she has seen the One who sees her.” Corpus-wide uniqueness claim is repeated but not substantiated.
fixes.proposed: Hagar, an enslaved Egyptian woman in the wilderness, addresses God as El Roi. The name is associated with seeing; the difficult words that follow connect her encounter with being seen by God.

fixes.wrong: “The verb "know" (də‘u) that follows is a Qal imperative for direct, experiential knowledge, not abstract information — the letting-go and the knowing are paired as one act: release your grip, and in doing so recognize who God is.” Parsing does not establish this epistemological distinction.
fixes.proposed: The commands ‘let go’ and ‘know that I am God’ stand together. In this psalm’s setting of conflict, they call listeners to cease striving and acknowledge God’s rule.

fixes.wrong: “The earliest manuscripts read simply "the one who keeps strengthening me" — later copies spell out "Christ," which is why many translations name him here.” No manuscript witnesses or dates supplied.
fixes.proposed: The Greek printed here says ‘the one who strengthens me,’ without naming him in this sentence. The study identifies him as Christ from the letter’s context. Paul’s ‘all things’ concerns the lack and plenty he has just described.

fixes.wrong: “Take one current difficulty you can't yet make sense of, and instead of demanding an explanation for it, entrust it specifically to God's ongoing work — not as a way of denying the pain, but as an act of trust that he is still working, even here.” Treats asking why as opposed to trust.
fixes.proposed: Bring God one difficulty you cannot make sense of. You may ask why and entrust it to him in the same prayer; neither requires calling the pain good.

fixes.wrong: “The present tense pictures an ongoing condition: these are people currently, continuously worn down, not merely tired on one occasion.” Parsing does not establish the exclusion.
fixes.proposed: The participle describes those who labor and are weary. The invitation names their burden without specifying how long they must have carried it.

fixes.wrong: “It does not demand that the throw happen once and never again; the psalm Peter echoes was prayed daily, and so is this.” Daily-use claims unsupported.
fixes.proposed: Nothing in the quoted instruction says that bringing anxiety to God may happen only once. Its reason remains available whenever we pray: he cares for us.

fixes.wrong: “Instead, rest for a moment in the plain fact stated here: you are in a saved condition right now, and it was given, not earned.” Assumes every app reader shares the addressed believers' standing.
fixes.proposed: If you trust Christ, let this assurance interrupt today’s performance scorekeeping: salvation is God’s gift. If you are exploring faith, notice the invitation to receive rather than earn.

fixes.wrong: “This is the mainstream reading among Greek grammarians (based on gender agreement, not theological preference), and it matters: the "gift" language covers the whole salvation-by-grace-through-faith reality, not one isolated piece of it.” Unsubstantiated consensus and excessive grammatical certainty; caution informed by my knowledge of debate.
fixes.proposed: A common reading takes ‘this’ to refer to the whole preceding statement. The gender difference supports that reading, but should not be presented as settling every question about faith and gift.

fixes.wrong: “This exact command — "be strong and courageous" — appears three times in this single chapter (vv. 6, 7, 9), each time grounded in a different reason.” Provisional knowledge-based check: verse 18 may add another occurrence; not supplied here.
fixes.proposed: In God’s opening commission, ‘be strong and courageous’ appears in verses 6, 7, and 9. The study draws attention to the different grounds for courage in those three statements.

fixes.wrong: “The Greek tense holds two things together at once — a decisive past event and its still-standing present result — which is exactly why Paul can say "I have been crucified" and "I live" in the same sentence without contradiction.” Tense cannot explain theological metaphor.
fixes.proposed: Paul places ‘I have been crucified with Christ’ beside ‘Christ lives in me.’ The contrast describes his present life through union with Christ’s death and life; the tense alone does not explain that mystery.

fixes.wrong: “Say aloud, as your own settled conviction and not just a hope: "I am convinced this cannot separate me from God's love."” Requires certainty the reader may not possess.
fixes.proposed: Read Paul’s assurance over that fear. If you cannot yet make his conviction your own, pray honestly: ‘Help me trust that this cannot separate me from your love in Christ.’

fixes.wrong: “This Greek word for "sound judgment" appears only this one time in the entire New Testament — its meaning has to be filled in from its close relatives, words for disciplined, sensible self-command.” Rarity does not establish that relatives must determine meaning.
fixes.proposed: Power, love, and sound judgment stand together against cowardice. In the letter’s call to faithful witness, the three belong together: strength to act, concern for others, and disciplined judgment.

fixes.wrong: “The verse closes Psalm 16 by returning to the "right hand" image from verse 8, where God's right hand was the place of support that kept David from being shaken; here it becomes the place of "pleasures forevermore" (נְעִמוֹת... נֶצַח).” Provisional knowledge-based check: verse 8 appears to place God at speaker's right hand; verse not supplied.
fixes.proposed: Here the psalmist locates enduring pleasures at God’s right hand. The image places joy in relationship with God.

fixes.wrong: “Sit for a minute today in silence and let this settle: this is God's posture toward his people, and in the Messiah you belong to them — he is not disappointed in you right now.” Rejoicing does not establish a personal verdict about every reader's conduct.
fixes.proposed: Sit for a minute with the promise that God rejoices over his people. Let his love welcome you into honest prayer, including repentance where it is needed.

fixes.wrong: “Then notice what being held feels like — on his timetable, not yours.” Implies felt peace is the eventual measure of trust.
fixes.proposed: You do not have to produce a feeling of peace. Let the spoken prayer be today’s act of trust, even if the anxious thought returns.

fixes.wrong: “Delight is something you're told to do, like fretting is something you're told to stop — and as delight in God grows, it reshapes what your heart wants in the first place, so that what you desire and what he gives begin to line up.” Desire-changing mechanism is an interpretation, not stated in the verse.
fixes.proposed: The promise belongs with the call to delight in the LORD. Many Christians understand that delight as reshaping desire; the verse itself does not explain exactly how desire and God’s giving relate.

fixes.wrong: “The next time grief or guilt threatens to be the last word, name one true thing about who God is that gives you a place to stand — and let that, not the feeling, be where you take refuge today.” Misses verse's concrete communal actions.
fixes.proposed: Receive one ordinary good thing with gratitude today, and share food or practical provision with someone who has little prepared. Let the celebration make room for another person.

fixes.wrong: “Love is defined entirely by what it does and refuses to do: staying patient rather than giving up on someone, choosing kindness, refusing to resent what someone else has, not needing to be seen as impressive.” Verbs do not prove entirely; overstates short list's scope.
fixes.proposed: Paul describes love through patience, kindness, and the refusal of envy, boasting, and pride. These qualities take practical shape in how we treat people.

fixes.wrong: “The verse pairs two different dwelling verbs — "sits" (settled residence) and "lodges" (the traveler's overnight shelter).” Leaves Shaddai unexplained while emphasizing a more speculative distinction.
fixes.proposed: Shaddai is a name for God, commonly rendered ‘the Almighty.’ Paired images of dwelling, shelter, and shadow picture life entrusted to his protection.

fixes.wrong: “Name one trial you're currently facing — a hardship you're going through, not harm someone is doing to you; that second thing isn't yours to reframe, it's something to get help with. For the trial that's actually yours to carry, ask 'what is this producing in me' instead of 'how do I escape this.'” Invents a division among trials and opposes endurance to seeking relief.
fixes.proposed: Name one hardship honestly. Ask God for endurance and for the help or relief you need. If someone is harming you, seek safety and support; this command does not require staying in harm or calling it good.

fixes.wrong: “Stillness here is chosen and commanded, not simply felt.” Turns self-address into an expectation of controllable inner stillness.
fixes.proposed: The psalmist directs his hope toward God while the threat remains. You can borrow that self-address without requiring your thoughts or feelings to become quiet immediately.

fixes.wrong: “Write down the boldest thing you can honestly ask God for in a situation you're facing — then pray it, leaving room for His answer to exceed not only the size of your request but the form you'd prefer it to take.” Risks converting ability into promise of superior requested outcome.
fixes.proposed: Bring God an honest request, and praise him for power beyond your understanding. Ask also for his strengthening within you; this praise does not promise that each request will receive a larger version of the answer you want.

fixes.wrong: “Take that step — a lamp doesn't show you the whole road, just enough to walk it, and that's the light this verse promises you today.” Contradicts card's refusal to specify amount of illumination.
fixes.proposed: Read a short passage of Scripture and identify one faithful action it makes clear. Take that step without requiring this verse to specify how much of the future God will show.

fixes.wrong: “"Seek first" picks up the seeking word Yeshua used two verses earlier for what the nations anxiously chase — food, drink, clothing — and redirects it: two closely related verbs, two completely different first objects of pursuit.” Study identifies verse 32, one verse earlier.
fixes.proposed: ‘Seek first’ answers the seeking described in the previous verse, redirecting attention from necessities toward God’s kingdom and righteousness.

fixes.wrong: “There's a difference between feeling free, claiming freedom, or being technically unshackled, and being genuinely free at the core.” Leaves bondage undefined. Proposed context relies on my knowledge of John 8:34 and needs verification.
fixes.proposed: In the surrounding discussion, Yeshua identifies slavery to sin. The Son’s freedom addresses that bondage; it is more specific than feeling independent or claiming freedom by status.

fixes.wrong: “Pesha is the sharpest of the three — it denotes willful breach or rebellion, a deliberate crossing of a known boundary, the language used of Israel's revolt against Moab (2 Kings 3:5) or a servant's break with a master, not an accidental slip.” Ranking conflicts with card; revolt direction doubtful from my knowledge, not verified here.
fixes.proposed: Here ‘transgressions’ names wrongdoing within the psalm’s wider language of sin and forgiveness. The emphasis is the completeness of God’s removal, not a ranked taxonomy of offenses.

fixes.wrong: “When your own ongoing struggle with sin tempts you toward self-condemnation, return to this verse as a legal fact, not a feeling: if you are in Christ, the verdict "guilty" no longer stands over you, regardless of how the daily battle is going.” Essay distinguishes no condemnation from innocence; Home card already improves this.
fixes.proposed: When your ongoing struggle with sin tempts you toward self-condemnation, return to this verse: if you are in Christ, no sentence of condemnation stands over you. You can acknowledge wrong honestly within that assurance.

fixes.wrong: “Joseph uses the identical Hebrew verb and structure for both "you intended" and "God intended" — naming two real, distinct intentions at work in the exact same events, without either one canceling the other.” Repeated verb suffices; identical structure unnecessarily overstates differently worded clauses.
fixes.proposed: Joseph repeats the verb ‘intended’ for his brothers and for God. He names their evil intention and God’s good purpose in the same events without calling the evil good.

fixes.wrong: The sentence beginning “This fits directly with what Paul has just said...” includes “and — continuing into the next verse — πίστις here best read as "faithfulness,"”. Supplied Greek and rendering already place faithfulness in verse 22.
fixes.proposed: Replace that portion with: and πίστις, rendered here as ‘faithfulness.’ The list continues in the following verse.

fixes.wrong: “Rather than picking one virtue from this list to force into existence today, spend a few minutes asking God what keeping in step with his Spirit would look like in this day's actual demands — and trust the fruit to grow from that walking.” Opposes intentional practice to reliance on Spirit.
fixes.proposed: Ask the Spirit to guide one concrete response today—perhaps patience in a conversation or kindness to a neighbor. Practice it in dependence on him; his fruit and your responsive action belong together.

fixes.wrong: “This is a Hifil (causative) imperfect of כון (kun, "to be firm, fixed, established"), the same root that appeared two verses earlier in 16:3, where committing one's works to the LORD results in plans being konon, "established."” Verse 3 is six verses before verse 9.
fixes.proposed: The study connects this verb with the language of plans being established earlier in the chapter, in 16:3.

fixes.wrong: “Given what precedes it (Exodus 14:13's "stand firm and see"), the stillness commanded here is the same posture: don't strategize, don't cry out in panic, don't take matters into your own hands.” Silence does not establish a ban on planning; card supplies forward-motion context.
fixes.proposed: Moses calls Israel to trust the LORD’s deliverance. The next verse’s command to move forward shows that keeping silence here is compatible with obedient action.

fixes.wrong: “Before your next act of worship or service, pause and ask honestly whether it flows from genuine loyalty to God or has become routine performance — then bring the actual relationship back into it.” Routine can embody faithful commitment; repetition is not the problem.
fixes.proposed: Before your next act of worship or service, ask whether any part of your conduct contradicts the loyalty you profess. Bring that honestly to God and choose one corresponding act of faithfulness.
